On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

title: ADAPT: Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing
summary: Retrieval-based classifiers efficiently route queries to specialised services, but they typically select a candidate even when no suitable service exists. We introduce Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing (ADAPT), a lightweight routing architecture with an explicit fallback option that enables queries to abstain from specialist selection. ADAPT uses the separation between the highest relevance score and the candidate score distribution as routing confidence. Experiments across retrieval models and increasing numbers of services reveal a consistent empirical behaviour: the confidence distribution changes systematically with candidate-pool size K, making fixed abstention thresholds increasingly miscalibrated. ADAPT addresses this effect with a K-aware threshold that adapts as services are added without classifier retraining. Evaluation across two specialist datasets shows that this simple mechanism provides an effective accuracy-cost trade-off compared with generative LLM routing, supporting lightweight and dynamically extensible service-routing architectures.

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

title: SAM 3 Sees More Than It Detects: Promptable Concept Maps Beyond Categories
summary: Promptable segmenters answer what a thing is. Dense prediction tasks also ask class-agnostic questions, such as what stands out or hides, how light is blocked, transmitted or reflected, and where structure lies. Robots, surveillance systems and image editors build on their answers. We study promptable concept maps (PCM), which extend SAM 3's promptable concept segmentation from noun instances to maps of concepts named by short noun phrases such as `"transparent object", with "none" as an answer. PCM-Bench groups the standard test sets of seven such tasks by the question they ask. On it, we find that SAM 3 sees more than it detects. Its semantic path responds to many of these concepts, yet a low image-level presence score can block every detection of its instance path. We present UNVEIL, which trains a copy of SAM 3's semantic path for these maps, with LoRA on copies of its last blocks. A separate presence decoder learns from verified negatives whether a concept occurs. With one text phrase per query, UNVEIL maps region concepts such as salient and camouflaged objects, shadows, transparent objects and mirrors. The same weights map thin structures such as edges and skeletons as well as object categories. Run next to SAM 3, it leaves SAM 3's own outputs unchanged. On each of the seven tasks, UNVEIL reaches the highest score among the compared promptable models, including SAM 3's official fine-tuning and pipelines built on multimodal LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/yuhuan-wu/UNVEIL.

title: Verification Behavior Across Five Qwen2.5-Instruct Checkpoints
summary: We evaluate five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) under four prompting conditions using three fixed tasks per information condition and five generations per task. Two AI raters scored 600 trajectories. Under the coordinated instruction, both raters recorded strict declarations of insufficiency in 11/15 cases at 7B, 0/15 at 14B, and 5/15 at 32B. The runner sent a standard follow-up when a request detector fired. The three checkpoints received at least one follow-up in 15, 12, and 15 cases, respectively. On information-sufficient tasks at 3B through 32B, scored format markers appeared in 60/60 protocol trajectories and 0/60 baseline trajectories. After adjudication, 1/60 in each condition met the diagnostic-execution criterion (H3). Across all checkpoints and prompts, 7/300 information-sufficient trajectories met H3 after adjudication, all on the same task. The prespecified upward transition did not occur in this run. The results separate visible structure, diagnostic execution, and persistence after a request for evidence.

title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
summary: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

title: An LLM-Driven Traffic-Control xApp for Dynamic 5G RAN Intents
summary: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.

title: PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing
summary: PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework that converts unstructured research materials into complete LaTeX manuscripts with literature synthesis and visual elements, outperforming existing autonomous writing systems in human evaluations.

title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
summary: TokenEconomizer reduces recurring token costs of coding agents across sequential real-world tasks by pruning irrelevant tools, injecting micro-skills, and interrupting failure loops.

title: π^4: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
summary: This unified foundation model enables the recovery of dense geometry, camera poses, and object tracking from diverse, uncalibrated observations in 4D scenes using a shared geometry and motion branch architecture.

title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
summary: Gamer is a generalist agent framework that integrates perception, memory, and multi-step reasoning, trained through continued pre-training, sparse-thinking instruction tuning, and multi-turn reinforcement learning to interact efficiently in 2D and 3D environments.

title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
summary: Edge0 enables efficient mixture-of-experts inference on consumer hardware by predicting expert routing ahead of time and using recovery adapters to maintain quality with minimal active memory.

title: Bitnet.cpp: Efficient Edge Inference for Ternary LLMs
summary: Bitnet.cpp enhances edge inference for ternary LLMs using a novel mixed-precision matrix multiplication library, achieving significant speed improvements over baselines.

title: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework
summary: A multi-agent framework using large language models for stock trading simulates real-world trading firms, improving performance metrics like cumulative returns and Sharpe ratio.

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
summary: Harness² improves agent execution harnesses through recursive task-level refinement and continual harness-level learning, boosting performance across benchmarks without ground-truth verifiers.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
summary: PagedAttention algorithm and vLLM system enhance the throughput of large language models by efficiently managing memory and reducing waste in the key-value cache.

title: OpenDevin: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents
summary: OpenDevin is a platform for developing AI agents that interact with the world by writing code, using command lines, and browsing the web, with support for multiple agents and evaluation benchmarks.

title: MinerU2.5: A Decoupled Vision-Language Model for Efficient High-Resolution Document Parsing
summary: MinerU2.5, a 1.2B-parameter document parsing vision-language model, achieves state-of-the-art recognition accuracy with computational efficiency through a coarse-to-fine parsing strategy.

title: Very Large-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation in AgentScope
summary: Enhancements to the AgentScope platform improve scalability, efficiency, and ease of use for large-scale multi-agent simulations through distributed mechanisms, flexible environments, and user-friendly tools.

title: AgentScope 1.0: A Developer-Centric Framework for Building Agentic Applications
summary: AgentScope enhances agentic applications by providing flexible tool-based interactions, unified interfaces, and advanced infrastructure based on the ReAct paradigm, supporting efficient and safe development and deployment.

title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
summary: Mem0, a memory-centric architecture with graph-based memory, enhances long-term conversational coherence in LLMs by efficiently extracting, consolidating, and retrieving information, outperforming existing memory systems in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: ARIS: Autonomous Research via Adversarial Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: ARIS is an open-source research harness that uses cross-model adversarial collaboration to ensure reliable long-term research outcomes through coordinated execution, orchestration, and assurance layers.

title: HuggingFace's Transformers: State-of-the-art Natural Language Processing
summary: Transformers library provides state-of-the-art Transformer architectures and pretrained models for natural language processing tasks with a unified API and emphasis on extensibility and robust deployment.

title: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate
summary: Jeveration repurposes a frozen vision-language model to generate coherent images and perform image-to-image and dense prediction tasks in a single forward pass with fast 512x512 generation.

title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
summary: LingBot-Touch is a tactile foundation model that learns a unified, extensible representation across heterogeneous tactile sensors, yielding plug-and-play tactile tokens that consistently enhance manipulation policies such as diffusion policy and VLA models.

title: Kronos: A Foundation Model for the Language of Financial Markets
summary: Kronos, a specialized pre-training framework for financial K-line data, outperforms existing models in forecasting and synthetic data generation through a unique tokenizer and autoregressive pre-training on a large dataset.

title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
summary: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
summary: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
summary: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce MedJev, a system one vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, MedJev removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of 7.93\% and a 6.04times end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that MedJev-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

title: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6: Expanding the Frontier of Document Parsing with Under-Optimized Region Refinement and Progressive Post-Training
summary: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 enhances document parsing performance through targeted data optimization and progressive post-training techniques, achieving state-of-the-art results on OmniDocBench v1.6.

title: SmolDocling: An ultra-compact vision-language model for end-to-end multi-modal document conversion
summary: SmolDocling is a compact vision-language model that performs end-to-end document conversion with robust performance across various document types using 256M parameters and a new markup format.

title: VibeVoice Technical Report
summary: VibeVoice synthesizes long-form multi-speaker speech using next-token diffusion and a highly efficient continuous speech tokenizer, achieving superior performance and fidelity.

title: Native and Compact Structured Latents for 3D Generation
summary: A new sparse voxel representation called O-Voxel enables high-quality 3D generative modeling with efficient inference and robust topology handling.

title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
summary: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

title: Ultralytics YOLO26: Unified Real-Time End-to-End Vision Models
summary: YOLO26 addresses real-time vision challenges through a unified model family with NMS-free inference, improved training strategies, and multi-task capabilities spanning detection, segmentation, and pose estimation.

title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

title: OmniFlatten: An End-to-end GPT Model for Seamless Voice Conversation
summary: A novel GPT-based model, OmniFlatten, enables real-time natural full-duplex spoken dialogue through a multi-stage post-training technique that integrates speech and text without altering the original model's architecture.

metadata.readme_excerpt: Paritok A non-destructive compression gateway for coding agents — cut your input-token bill without changing your agent. Paritok sits between your agent and the LLM as a drop-in proxy. On every request it strips the tool-schema bloat, compresses tool results and file reads, and summarizes stale history — then forwards upstream, billed on the compressed tokens. Nothing is ever permanently discarded: the agent pulls back any exact original on demand. Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenHands , and any agent that honors BASE_URL — you don't change a line of your agent . Powered by the first open-source 4B compression model trained specifically for coding agents (45K real agent trajectories). Cut input token bills from ~25% on turn one to past 85% in long, context-saturated sessions , and fit ~3× more turns in the same context window. metadata.readme_excerpt: ![Caveman Compression](images/banner.png) **Lossless semantic compression for LLM contexts** [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![Python 3.8+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.8+-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [Quick Start](#quick-start) • [Examples](#examples) • [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) • [Spec](SPEC.md) --- ## What is this? Strip grammar. Keep facts. Save tokens. ```diff - "In order to optimize the database query performance, we should consider implementing an index on the frequently accessed columns..." (70 tokens) + "Need fast queries. Check which columns used most. Add index to those columns..." (50 tokens) = 29% reduction ``` --- ## How It Works ![How Caveman Compression Works](images/info.png) LLMs excel at filling linguistic gaps. They predict missing grammar, connectives, and structure. **Key insight:** We remove only what LLMs can reliably reconstruct. **What we remove (predictable):** - Grammar: "a", "the", "is", "are" - Connectives: "therefore", "however", "because" - Passive constructions: "is calculated by" - Filler words: "very", "quite", "essentially" **What we keep (unpredictable):** - Facts: numbers, names, dates - Technical terms: "O(log n)", "binary search" - Constraints: "medium-large", "frequently accessed" - Specifics: "Stockholm", "99.9% uptime" ``` Compressed: "Company medium-large. Location Stockholm." Decompressed: "at a medium-large company based in Stockholm" ↑ grammar added, facts unchanged ↑ ``` --- ## Quick Start ### Installation **LLM-based (best compression, requires OpenAI API):** ```bash python3 -m venv venv source venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt # Set up API key cp .env.example .env # Edit .env and add your OpenAI API key ``

metadata.readme_excerpt: Context Engine Semantic code search, memory, and symbol intelligence for AI coding assistants. Get your free account at dev.context-engine.ai Website · Get Started · License --- ## Install Skills Context Engine ships AI agent skills that teach your coding assistant how to use 30+ MCP tools for semantic search, symbol graph navigation, memory, and more. **Guidance:** Recommend pasting this into your project's `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` to reach subagents: ```markdown # Context Engine When the `context-engine` MCP server is connected, this workspace is indexed: for any question about the codebase, call `repo_search` FIRST, before ls/find/Grep/Read, and again whenever you move to a new area; for how/why questions that span several files use `context_answer`. Results are verified source with exact line ranges: treat them as already read. Use Grep only to confirm an exact literal in a file you already know, or to count. For questions asking for every/all sites, run one repo_search per distinct pattern (queries=[...]) and follow the refs. If the tools are listed as deferred, load them with ToolSearch first. | Need | Tool | |---|---| | Find code by behavior, concept, error text or identifier | `repo_search` (`queries=[...]` for several at once; `under`, `language`, `path_glob` to narrow) | | Explain how/why across several files, with citations | `context_answer` | | Definition, callers, callees, importers, references of a symbol | `symbol_graph` (several names: `A\|B\|C`) | | Multi-hop impact before a change | `graph_query` | | Code that may live in another indexed repo | `cross_repo_search` | Before editing, fetch every involved symbol in one call; before a rename or signature change, get every site with `symbol_graph` `query_type=references`. Search again only after learning

metadata.readme_excerpt: Long-term memory for AI assistants — fast, private, and yours. # AutoMem [AutoMem](https://automem.ai) gives your AI a memory that survives the chat. Save the decisions, preferences, notes, and context that matter. The next time you open Claude, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, or another connected assistant, it can bring back the right details instead of making you repeat yourself. Ask, "Why did we choose PostgreSQL?" and AutoMem can return the decision, the alternatives you considered, the principle behind it, and the work that followed — not just a pile of similarly worded snippets. ## Why AutoMem feels different **No LLM call in the middle of recall.** AutoMem looks up memories directly through its graph and vector index. That keeps normal retrieval fast and avoids an extra generative-LLM charge every time your assistant needs context. It still uses embeddings — from Voyage, OpenAI, or a local provider — and optional enrichment can add more structure over time. **More than vector search.** A vector match finds something similar; AutoMem also records typed relationships between memories. It can follow the connections between a decision, its rationale, and its consequences, so your assistant has a better chance of returning the *why*, not only the words it recognizes. **One memory across your tools.** Use the local MCP bridge with Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and more. For cloud agents, Remote MCP connects the same service to ChatGPT Developer Mode, Claude.ai, and ElevenLabs over HTTPS. Your memory is not locked to one chat app. **Own the data and the setup.** Run AutoMem locally with Docker, on your own infrastructure, or as a small Railway service group. It exposes both MCP and a REST API, so it fits into the tools and workflows you already use. ## Pr

title: A Brief Overview of Non-Terrestrial Networks (Updated 2026)
summary: This article extends the 2023 preprint \emph{A brief introduction to satellite communications for Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN)} (\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04590v1}{arXiv:2305.04590v1}) with a revision of its foundations, tables and state of the art as of 18 November 2026. It revisits propagation, link budgets, spectrum reuse and phased arrays, including corrected equations and numerical examples. Updated tables distinguish operational, launched and planned constellations and compare published fixed-terminal rates with direct-to-device services. The discussion incorporates developments in 3GPP Releases 17--20, commercial LTE-based direct-to-cell services and research towards 6G non-terrestrial networks. Operator announcements are distinguished from independent measurements and future plans. Open challenges include spectrum coordination, Doppler and timing compensation, mobility, capacity, security and the sustainability of low Earth orbit.

title: Kameleo: In-Situ Activation-Precision Selection for Bit-Serial LLM Accelerators
summary: Weight-only quantization keeps the activations of large language models (LLMs) in a higher-precision format, pushing the on-chip inference cost to the activation arithmetic. Bit-serial, variable-length accelerators offer a promising path to reduce this cost by lowering activation precision while preserving model quality. They process only the mantissa bits that each layer needs. The length has to be chosen per layer and operator, and today it is chosen by offline calibration: a search driven by the perplexity of the full model on a representative dataset. The search is repeated for every model and workload, and its result degrades silently on other data. This paper presents Kameleo, an accelerator that selects the activation precision at runtime, on the accelerator, from the data it is processing. Kameleo replaces the global perplexity by a local proxy that compares the output of each GEMM at reduced and at full precision. It exploits the fact that a bit-serial datapath produces this comparison almost for free, because the reduced-precision result is an intermediate state of the full-precision computation. Two passes over the first tokens of a workload set the precision of every GEMM. On four LLMs and seven datasets, Kameleo stays within a 1% perplexity budget at a 2.11-2.34x reduction of prefill cycles on the matrix multiplication unit (MXU), close to the reduction of configurations calibrated offline on the evaluation data itself. Calibrated configurations transferred to other data, in contrast, often violate the budget. The selection hardware adds only 3.7% to the accelerator area. Kameleo thereby makes variable-length mantissas feasible in real deployments, where offline calibration for every model and workload is not.

title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing
summary: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.

title: CRAFT: Analog Circuit Design by Reasoning LLM Agents from Pre-Computed Lookup Tables
summary: Automated analog circuit sizing methods, from black-box optimizers to recent large language model (LLM) agents, typically search the design space with a SPICE simulator in the loop, whereas an experienced designer works out a design by hand analysis. This paper presents CRAFT, a flow in which an LLM agent designs a given topology by calculation, as a designer does, and without an initial sizing. The agent works only through DeX, a service that uses pre-computed lookup tables to provide device characteristics and to solve the whole netlist for its operating point and small-signal response. It thus designs without SPICE, and every final design is verified independently in HSPICE. We test CRAFT on four circuits in a commercial 28 nm process; the largest is a 37-transistor three-stage amplifier with 53 design variables, 20 specifications and 74 saturation constraints. With Claude Opus 5.5, CRAFT meets every specification and constraint in all 20 runs, five per circuit. On that amplifier, with DeX in place of HSPICE and an identical request for both, the same agent passes in 10 of 10 runs instead of 6 of 10 within an hour and is 2.0x faster at the median.

title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
summary: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.

title: Software-Defined Internet Integration of Satellite Networks (SDISN)
summary: This paper proposes SDISN, a software-defined Internet integration of satellite networks. It facilitates the transmission of IP traffic from user terminals (UTs) or Internet nodes over a satellite network with inter-satellite links (ISLs). Gateways (GWs) together with Points of Presence (PoPs) support the transition between the satellite network and the Internet. UTs and GWs connect to the satellite network via serving satellites (SrvSats). As the satellites orbit the Earth at high speed, UTs and GWs frequently change their SrvSats. This causes frequent changes to their reachability, which poses a major challenge for integration. In the proposed solution, GWs and SrvSats encapsulate traffic with forwarding information so that the traffic can be carried over the satellite network towards appropriate SrvSats of UTs or GWs. The forwarding information on the encapsulating nodes is continuously updated by a controller to reflect changed SrvSats and possibly changed topology of the satellite network. Design goals for the proposed architecture were low complexity on satellites, high ability for traffic engineering, and keeping UTs out of the routing system for security and compatibility reasons. UTs may have increased security requirements (ISRs) such that their traffic should be carried within the constellation to avoid non-trusted terrestrial infrastructure. Extensions are proposed to support such ISRs. UTs may obtain either dynamic IP addresses from a nearby GW/PoP wherever they roam or they may obtain static IP addresses from a fixed Home GW/PoP. In the latter case, triangle routing via the Home GW occurs when the UT roams away from the Home GW. As this adds latency to the communication, we investigate architectural extensions for latency reduction. In addition, we show how traffic engineering can be performed in such an architecture with the help of alternate GWs and SrvSats.

title: An LLM-Driven Traffic-Control xApp for Dynamic 5G RAN Intents
summary: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.

title: Mitigating Row Buffer Contention Through Multiple Row Buffer (MRB) DRAM
summary: DRAM chips contain multiple banks to handle sev- eral memory requests in parallel. However, requests to different rows of the same bank (e.g., from different cores or workload access patterns) interfere with each other by contending for a single shared row buffer. This introduces row buffer conflicts, which incur performance and energy overheads. In this work, we reduce row buffer conflicts caused by interference by introducing multiple row buffers in each bank. We propose multiple row buffer (MRB) DRAM, which employs a primary global row buffer along with multiple secondary SRAM row buffers in the DRAM chip. These secondary SRAM row buffers act as a cache that enables each bank to serve requests to multiple rows in parallel, thereby improving performance and reducing row buffer conflicts. Our evaluation shows that MRB-DRAM with four SRBs per bank improves performance by an average of 29.7%, 24% in singlecore, multicore systems, respectively, compared to a conventional DDR4 baseline with a modest area overhead of 2%.

title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair
summary: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

title: Intent-Defined Radio: A Goal-Native Architecture for Next-Generation Wireless Networks
summary: Wireless systems are becoming harder to operate because service goals are increasingly expressed in outcome-oriented terms, while radio platforms still expose mainly low-level configurations and protocol-specific controls. This mismatch makes it difficult to translate latency, reliability, throughput, and continuity requirements into coherent radio behavior. This article argues for Intent-Defined Radio (IDR) as a new system abstraction for next-generation wireless networks. Rather than treating the radio stack as a fixed mechanism set to be manually engineered and then tuned, IDR connects explicit service goals to executable radio behavior within a constrained design space by leveraging the capacity of large language models (LLMs). We position IDR relative to programmable radio, intent-based networking, and learning-based protocol design. We also present two simulation studies using Intent2MAC to illustrate the design loop, demonstrating executable MAC synthesis and offline refinement guided by evaluation feedback. The results show improved service satisfaction at a throughput cost and improved remote-control performance when random contention is replaced by distributed urgency-based arbitration. We finally discuss the open challenges in intent specification, evidence, hardware execution, interoperability, and lifecycle cost, and outline a staged path toward deployment.

title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
summary: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.

title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash
summary: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.

title: ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that translate user requests into sequences of local tool invocations. While prior cache-based side-channel attacks target the locally deployed models, they typically require the adversary to share model-related components or hardware resources with the victim's inference process. These assumptions do not apply to the predominant agentic settings, in which commercial LLMs execute on vendor-controlled infrastructure. We show that agentic execution exposes a more practical attack surface: although inference remains remote, tools are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe for monitoring agentic tool invocations. Our evaluation across three hardware platforms shows that Flush+Reload enables accurate, real-time tool monitoring, whereas Prime+Probe, despite supporting cross-VM attacks, incurs prohibitive monitoring overhead and suffers from cache-set aliasing. We present ToolPulse, a cache-based side-channel eavesdropping framework against tool-using agents. We first design the Tool Recovery Attack to reconstruct an agent's tool-execution workflow. We evaluate the Tool Recovery Attack on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code. It consistently reconstructs tool workflows, with the lowest F1 score exceeding 93%. We further demonstrate two attack scenarios enabled by the recovered traces. Task Profiling Attack infers user intent across two Terminal-Bench task categories and the Trigger Localization Attack identifies sensitive tool calls in encryption/decryption and model training/inference workloads. Even under substantial system noise on a server shared by approximately 20 users, both Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack maintain high accuracy.

title: BOOMerang: Autonomous Translation from RTL to Microarchitectural Simulators and Back
summary: High-level simulators like gem5 are often used to test and demonstrate novel architectural techniques. While these simulators provide high research productivity, they generally lack the means to provide detailed feedback on the realizability of a hardware design. Furthermore, these simulators can frequently fall out-of-sync with the detailed performance characteristics of real hardware designs, which is usually the responsibility of dedicated engineers/teams in industry. While RTL implementation can address these challenges, it can be even more difficult to translate simulator code to high-quality RTL by hand without a large team. In this work, we architect and evaluate agentic loops that automate both parts of the RTL vs. high-level simulator workflow that is critical to high-quality architecture research. Our loops (1) automatically generate accurate high-level models of RTL implementations of CPU designs (BOOM) in a battle-tested microarchitecture simulation framework (gem5) and (2) automatically translate new microarchitectural features implemented in the high-level simulator back to RTL faithfully. Targeting the first loop at autonomously building a gem5 model for the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM) core, we generate a simulator with IPC within 3% of the RTL, meeting targets pursued for simulators in industry, in only 2 days. We use our second loop to automatically translate 72 features from this aligned gem5 simulator into RTL in the BOOM core, while maintaining its low IPC error. Combining translated optimizations together yields a 25% performance improvement for the BOOM core RTL implementation in SPECint 2017, demonstrating that having these loops for moving between high-level simulation and RTL enables actual improvement of processor performance. The agentic loops we developed and the simulators and RTL we generated will be available in open-source.

title: SGLayout: Schema-Guided Closed-Loop Refinement for LLM-Driven Parameterized Layout Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that closes this gap via a schema-guided mechanism. Upon code execution, a structured schema captures the correspondence between each code-level instance and its geometric attributes, establishing a bidirectional link between code space and geometry space. Emulating engineer review practices, SGLayout evaluates layouts along two complementary dimensions: intent compliance through quantitative structural checking and qualitative vision-language assessment, and rule compliance through DRC. All identified violations are then back-projected through the schema onto precise code targets, enabling surgical repair. This closed-loop process iterates until layout convergence. On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.

title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
summary: Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 $μ$s per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.

title: FPGA-GEN: Target-Aware RTL Generation via HLS
summary: Successful C/C++ compilation does not guarantee correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS). FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions. On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task yield 407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes. In a cumulative conversion campaign, FPGA-GEN admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation, Vivado synthesis/fit, and same-RTL evidence. In focused TensorCore screening, selected candidate 3 reports 73.7% fewer CSynth cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than generated/composed C0, with 26.7% more DSPs, and passes development CoSim.

title: SimPyWireless: A PHY-Aware Discrete-Event Simulation Framework for Wi-Fi and 5G NR-U Coexistence in the 5 GHz Band
summary: The growing demand from heterogeneous wireless applications with stringent QoS and QoE requirements is increasing pressure on available spectrum resources. Although mmWave and THz bands offer additional capacity, their propagation and hardware limitations make sub-6~GHz unlicensed spectrum, particularly the 5~GHz band, an attractive complementary resource. However, reproducible Wi-Fi/5G NR-U coexistence studies remain limited by the lack of lightweight, open-source, PHY-aware simulation platforms. We present SimPyWireless, a discrete-event simulation framework for Wi-Fi and 5G NR-U coexistence in the 5~GHz unlicensed band. The framework integrates shared-channel modeling, propagation, interference, SINR, heterogeneous traffic, mobility, and technology-specific channel access, while providing modular support for externally trained AI/ML models. We validate SimPyWireless against an analytical DTMC model and demonstrate expected coexistence behavior under varying contention and mobility conditions. SimPyWireless provides a reproducible and extensible middle ground between analytical modeling and hardware-based experimentation.

title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
summary: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.

title: ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design
summary: Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

title: RE-CAM: Readout-Enhanced Content-Addressable Memory for Quantitative Similarity Search
summary: Similarity search is essential to many applications but incurs massive data movement when executed on conventional architectures. Content-addressable memory (CAM) is a promising hardware substrate, as it allows similarity search directly in the CAM array, minimizing data movement and offering both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, conventional CAM array readout produces only binary match results, discarding quantitative similarity information that could be further exploited. Extracting this information requires interpreting the CAM array output voltage that evolves during a CAM search, making the sensing timestamp a crucial design variable alongside the reference voltage and decoding parameter. In this work, we propose RE-CAM, a readout enhancement framework for CAM that is agnostic to memory technology and application, enabling CAM array readout to approximate linear and nonlinear functions with one CAM search. By reusing the comparators to sense the time-varying output voltage multiple times, jointly optimizing the three design variables under system constraints and hardware nonidealities, and co-designing the optimization algorithm and reconfigurable hardware, RE-CAM achieves accurate approximation with low energy and area overhead without introducing a readout throughput bottleneck. Across linear, piecewise-linear, sigmoid, and exponential functions, RE-CAM reduces normalized root mean square error by 10.89% to 24.34% for general approximation and 29.43% to 46.73% when exploiting dataset distribution, compared to a shared uniform-reference ADC baseline with the same comparison budget. Relative to the same baseline, RE-CAM also achieves $8\times$ higher search throughput while reducing energy per search and area by 47% and 39%, respectively.

title: Verified Netlist-to-RTL Recovery with LLM Agents
summary: Gate-level netlists circulate among IP integrators and foundries and can be extracted from chips. Reverse engineering them into readable register-transfer-level (RTL) code would help an adversary understand and modify a design, but remains difficult because word-level operations are scattered across many gates. Large language models (LLMs) can write and optimize RTL, but often fail to recover it from a whole netlist. We propose LOCA (LOgic Cone Attack), an LLM-based attack that divides an anonymized netlist into logic cones, has parallel agents rewrite them, and assembles compact RTL. Each cone contains the complete next-state logic of a group of related registers, giving an agent a small, meaningful task. Of five partitioning methods tested, only grouped cones lead to recovery. LOCA keeps only RTL proven equivalent to the netlist and measures its quality by compression. Function-preserving obfuscation does not stop LOCA on the tested designs, whereas unknown keys or hidden cell functions prevent it from proving recovery of the original design. Across 21 model-design pairs, LOCA recovers 17, versus 6 with whole-netlist prompting. Per-run recovery across models rises from 5% to 74%, at a median cost below one dollar with a low-cost model.

title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
summary: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

title: Bottom-Up FPGA Reconfigurable Accelerator Overlay Generation
summary: Programmable FPGA overlays run new workloads without re-synthesis, yet they pay twice. An overlay adds a second layer of programmability on top of the FPGA's own overhead. Moreover, overlay generators usually start from a regular template, so they spend logic on switches and links that the workloads never use, and they close timing at low clocks. We present a flow that instead grows an overlay bottom-up from the dataflow graphs of the workloads it must run. The flow clusters workloads by structural similarity, ranks shared slots with spectral descriptors of each operation's surroundings, and adds only the units and links a workload lacks. It builds every unit on native hard blocks, with their internal pipeline registers, dual-ported memories and double-pumped DSPs, and it uses fixed-function engines where wider data types exceed the overlay's 16-bit lanes. Workloads then switch by configuration alone. On an AMD VCK5000, across 17 workloads from three suites and against OverGen rebuilt for the same board, our images run at 250-400 MHz instead of 35-50 MHz. As a result, they are 9.52-10.33x faster in geometric mean, and up to 36.97x, while using 19.4-22.1x less of the FPGA and 9.67-10.51x less estimated board energy.

title: Native FPGA Hard-Block Implementation from High-Level Synthesis
summary: High-level synthesis (HLS) maps computations to FPGA hard blocks, yet often leaves their arithmetic modes, internal registers, and cascade links idle and recreates them in the fabric, costing area and timing. We present a C++ template library that reaches native hard-block implementations without modifying the HLS compiler. Templates fix source patterns, and an automatic flow picks scheduling settings and verified RTL patches. On AMD Versal, our matrix multiplication uses 2.4--4.5x fewer lookup tables (LUTs) than AutoSA systolic arrays at equal or higher estimated throughput. Our INT8 matrix--vector units reach the three multiply--accumulates per DSP of hand-written FINN RTL, versus at most 1.29 for HLS libraries. In hls4ml, Allo, and Stream-HLS, the templates cut LUTs by up to 2.7x and DSPs by up to 2x.

title: Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization for Bitcoin Custody
summary: A compromised cryptocurrency withdrawal backend can request signatures on unauthorized payments. Previously signed transactions may remain spendable after pause or become spendable again after a reorganization. Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization (RBWA) orders permits against pause in a replicated journal and restores exposure when its closing evidence disappears from Bitcoin's active chain. An optional route delays large payouts and permits independent cold recovery. Direct payments confirm in one block on regtest, and staged payments confirm in three or seven at delays of two or six. After rollback, a replayed recovery can win or lose to an already exported mature payout. Authenticated receipts can revoke one signing lease in a shared wallet. In matched synthetic schedules, probes reduce permits through compromised leases from 20 to 9 out of 33, with one false fence. Two held-out HTTP workloads find equal fixed-threshold precision for boosted audit and probe-augmented detectors. The audit fields already expose the probe authentication outcome. Live tests verify an exact maintenance exception and add a file marker as a distinct source. The marker fences a compromised lease that RPC-only audit misses. Audit with the same file-read evidence also fences a reader who bypasses the probe. The results tie the benefit of active probing to which evidence the operator can obtain.

title: Benchmarking Open-Source O-RAN and 5G NTN Stacks on Embedded ARM Platforms for Space Payloads
summary: Regenerative satellite payloads, which host the 5G Next Generation Node B (gNB) onboard instead of transparently relaying the radio signal, are a key building block of the Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) integration that 3GPP started in Release 17. Combining them with the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture adds software-defined control through RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs), enabling in-orbit reconfiguration, multi-tenancy, and data-driven radio resource management. Open-source implementations make this vision accessible to research institutions and New Space missions, yet there is little quantitative evidence on how they behave on the embedded processors that a satellite can actually carry. This paper presents an out-of-the-box experimental benchmark of two open-source gNB stacks (i.e., OpenAirInterface/Duranta and srsRAN/OCUDU), and two Near-Real-Time RICs (i.e., the ORAN-SC Near-RT RIC and FlexRIC). All components are deployed on an ARMv8 platform representative of the processing units used in small-satellite payloads, driving a USRP B210 software-defined radio. We compare them in terms of functional compliance (3GPP NTN features, O-RAN interfaces, multi-tenancy), resource efficiency, real-time behavior, and engineering suitability. Results show that these platforms can host a joint gNB + near-RT RIC deployment using any of the considered components, although further optimizations are still required for carrier-grade performance. However, the performance and standards compliance vary significantly among them. Building on these results, we derive a decision framework that maps mission profiles and Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) budgets to gNB/near-RT RIC combinations. Finally, we discuss the open gaps remaining before these stacks can be flown in NTN regenerative payloads.

title: CAIMS: Scalable Cross-Array In-Memory Search
summary: Search, especially top-k similarity search, plays a vital role in many applications, but its performance can be severely limited by memory access overhead. In-memory search (IMS), an alternative to CPU/GPU-based approaches, exploits massive parallelism within a content-addressable memory (CAM) array to perform search in situ and provides both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, the capacity of a single CAM array is often insufficient for modern workloads, requiring data to be distributed across multiple arrays. Deploying scalable top-k similarity search across multiple CAM arrays poses a fundamental problem that existing designs fail to address: how to accurately and efficiently reduce local binary match results to global top-k results. This work introduces CAIMS, a cross-array IMS framework that is agnostic to memory technologies and applications, enabling scalable and efficient top-k similarity search while preserving accuracy. To enable accurate top-k result reduction, CAIMS leverages the existing threshold match functionality with a combined offline and online parameter selection approach to transform local binary match results that lack globally comparable similarity information into global coarse-grained similarity scores. To further improve efficiency, CAIMS conducts hierarchical reduction and transfers only the selection results and necessary control signals with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated using the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, CAIMS improves throughput by up to $22.3\times/10.1\times$ and energy efficiency by $426.6\times/23.7\times$ compared to the server-class CPU baseline and prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, respectively, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

title: TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect -- KV Cache Management for AI Agents
summary: LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference. To address this problem, we present \emph{TripleKV}, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. %exploits tool execution to hide these delays. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory. Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45--76\% to under 10\%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49\% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7$\times$ lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.

title: Berth: SLO-Preserving GPU Sharing Without New Preemption
summary: Inference services keep GPUs reserved for their worst-case load, and most of that capacity sits idle. Filling it with best-effort work such as training is the obvious remedy, and latency is why it rarely happens: on a shared GPU, a request that must finish within milliseconds finds the best-effort job's kernels running or queued ahead of it. Spatial sharing cannot evict them, temporal sharing gives the request only its turn, and hardware partitioning protects it by idling what it does not use. Systems that keep both the SLO and the utilization have reached inside the stack (rewriting kernels, patching the driver, instrumenting the framework), which the operator of a closed GPU stack cannot do. This paper argues that reaching inside is unnecessary. The time-slicer built into commodity GPUs already preempts a running kernel within a fraction of a millisecond and switches the moment a context runs out of work; what it lacks is priority, and priority can be created from outside by controlling what the best-effort context has to run. Berth is a user-space system built on this observation: a preloaded shim feeds the best-effort job to the GPU only when no request needs it (feed control), a declared deadline reference extends the rule to continuous-batching LLM engines, and a shortened best-effort time slice, set without privileges, bounds what a long kernel can cost. Berth changes no application, framework, kernel or driver. Across 31 scenario points with MLPerf SLOs and 13 baselines, Berth meets SLOs within a few percentage points of running alone, above every baseline, with 2.7-3.5x the best-effort throughput of the strongest ones; beside LLM serving, it meets per-token targets for nearly every request while training keeps running. Sharing a closed GPU under SLOs needs no new preemption mechanism, only control over what the existing one sees.

title: Twindex: Index Cache Offloading with Coarse-to-Fine Selection for Long-Context Sparse-Attention Serving
summary: In long-context decoding, GPU memory (HBM) caps how many requests a GPU decodes at once. Sparse-attention models such as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.2 add an indexer: at every step it scores all past index entries with its own indexer cache, and attention reads the main KV of only the top-k entries. We find that once serving systems move the main KV to host memory, the indexer cache becomes the HBM bottleneck, at 63% of per-request HBM on Qwen and 75% on V4.1 at 1M tokens. Therefore, we introduce Twindex, which keeps only a compact copy of the indexer cache in HBM and the full indexer cache in host memory. At each step, the copy selects a larger candidate set, and the model's own indexer picks the top-k from the original rows of the candidates in host memory. The copy combines the shared component with the compressed residuals, both learned once offline. Twindex changes no model weights and runs inside CUDA graphs. At 1M tokens on modern GPUs, Twindex fits $1.78\times$, $1.62\times$ and $3.03\times$ as many requests as KV offloading alone on Qwen, V4.1 and GLM-5.2, and reaches $1.44\times$, $1.25\times$ and $2.54\times$ decode throughput when host memory does not limit the batch. Every request keeps its own index, and Qwen and GLM requests share prefix main KV in host memory. In our evaluations, mean benchmark scores are at most 3.1% below the baseline's.

title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
summary: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.

title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
summary: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.

title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
summary: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs.
